title: Right of Way
passage:
The pass at Ferningate is a plain thing: nine concrete cross-walls in a chute let into the weir’s left abutment, each with a notch in it, and a trap in the top pool. The weir held water for a mill that stopped in 1931. Since the pass opened in 2011 the trap has been emptied most mornings of the run, the counts written into a hardbacked book. The first nine springs are in one hand, the rest in three others. Over fifteen springs the book records 6,140 brown trout, 288 grayling, 31 dace and nine chub. Nobody says the pass does not work. What has taken fifteen years to become interesting is what it works for. The river below it is thick with dace; one afternoon’s netting last May took four hundred-odd of them, more than the trap has held in fifteen years.

The explanation people reach for first is strength. The head is 2.4 metres and the fall from one pool to the next about 270 millimetres; a trout goes up without appearing to try, and a dace is a small fish. Elspeth Kelsingham, a fisheries biologist who spent two springs at the weir with tags and three antennas, thinks strength has little to do with it. She tagged 212 dace and released them 600 metres downstream. Two antennas lay on the apron at the weir’s foot, one each side; a third in the pass mouth. Within nine days 174 of them had been read at the weir, so they got there. Twenty-three of the 174 crossed the antenna on the left bank, where the entrance is. Nine went in. Five came out at the top, a sixth of all the dace in the book. “The dace aren’t beaten by the ladder,” she says. “They don’t find it, and they don’t find it because they don’t come up that side of the river.”

Her account turns on where a fish puts itself in moving water. A trout or a grayling holds in the current and works up the fastest thread of it, which here runs hard along the left bank and puts a fish at the weir beside the notch. Dace travel otherwise. They move up in loose shoals along the margins, and the right margin is a long slack behind a shingle bar. A fish that follows it arrives on the far side from the entrance, thirty metres of broken water away, with little to tell it anything is there. The pass releases about a quarter of a cubic metre a second; in April the river brings down nine. Four metres out from the mouth there is nothing of that quarter left to follow.

The grayling make a different case, and Kelsingham keeps them apart. Of 74 tagged, 61 reached the weir, 54 on the left, and 39 went into the pass, as a fish that lives in the current would. Twelve came out at the top. Whatever stops them is inside. A grayling is deep through the body and carries a dorsal fin like a sail, and it does not leave the water; to get up a notch it must swim through the jet, a few seconds of everything it has. Kelsingham split the entrants by temperature. Of the eleven that entered above ten degrees, seven got out; of the twenty-eight that entered colder, five did. The pools do not help. They are short, and at April flows the jet from one notch reaches the wall of the next; there is no quiet corner in them. A fish that misses is put back down the pool and starts again further behind.

Two springs is a small return for the work, and Kelsingham says so before anyone else does. “Ask me again when I’ve had five more springs of it,” she says. The antennas settled the question of where the fish came up, and she does not qualify that result. The temperature split she calls suggestive and no more. None of it speaks to the trout, which run in November and December when the river is high; in three of those fifteen winters it came over the crest deep enough to drown the weir out, and the book counts only what went through the trap. The remedy her argument points to is a second mouth on the right bank, where the bar has moved twice since 2011. What has been tried is smaller. In 2023 two of the nine cross-walls were cut with submerged orifices, 300 millimetres square, so a fish could go through a wall instead of over it. A spate in February packed the lower one to the top with gravel, and it is still packed. The other, three walls further up, came through the same water clear.
– Adrian Kitson

questions.prompt: What are we told about the counts kept in the book at the trap?

options.text: They begin in 1931, the year the mill that the weir was built to serve finally stopped.
One afternoon of netting below the weir took more dace than the trap has ever held.
Chub were written down as dace in the first few springs of the run.
Three of the four people who have kept the book wrote up the first nine springs.

questions.rationale:
B is right. The book holds 31 dace across fifteen springs, and a single afternoon’s netting in the river below the weir took four hundred-odd dace, which the passage says outright is more than the trap has held in fifteen years. The option puts that comparison in different words and adds nothing to it.

A takes a date that belongs to something else nearby. The mill stopped in 1931; the counts start when the pass opened in 2011. A reader skimming for a year finds the wrong one.

C is the answer shaped like a caveat about the record, and it is the trap for anyone who picks whichever option sounds properly careful about data. Nothing in the text raises any doubt about how the fish were told apart; chub and dace are simply two of the four species in the list. Sounding careful is not the same as being supported.

D has the four keepers right and their shares the wrong way round. One hand wrote the first nine springs; the three others share the remaining six. The option gives the long early stretch to three people and the short recent one to a single keeper.

questions.prompt: What are we told about the grayling in Kelsingham’s study?

options.text: The colder arrivals did about as well in the pass as the warmer ones.
The pools between the walls give them somewhere to rest as they climb.
Their size, rather than their build, is what holds them up in the pass.
Most of those that entered the pass did not reach its top pool.

questions.rationale:
D is right. Thirty-nine tagged grayling went into the pass and twelve came out at the top, so most of the fish that got in were stopped somewhere between the entrance and the top pool. That is the point of the paragraph: with the grayling the loss happens inside the structure.

A flattens the temperature split. Seven of the eleven that entered above ten degrees came out, against five of the twenty-eight that entered colder; the two groups did not fare alike, and the option asks the reader to treat them as though they did.

B names the thing a pool-and-weir pass is supposed to provide, and this one does not. The passage is blunt about it: the pools are too short for the jet at April flows, which carries from each notch as far as the wall below it, so no part of a pool is still. A fish that fails at a notch loses the pool it had gained and must begin again from further back, which is the opposite of rest.

C sounds like the text and is not what the text says. The difficulty is put down to build: a deep body, a dorsal fin like a sail, a fish that does not leave the water. Size is what the passage raises about the dace, and then sets aside.

questions.prompt: Why, in Kelsingham’s account, do so few dace get above the weir at Ferningate?

options.text: They come up the bank opposite the entrance, and too little flows from it to draw them over.
The fall from one pool to the next is more than a small fish can manage.
They run up the river earlier in the spring than the pass is opened for them.
They will not leave a shoal to make their way up a narrow channel one fish at a time.

questions.rationale:
A is right, and it has two halves because the account has two. Dace work upstream along the margins, and at this weir that lands them on the right, thirty metres of broken water from an entrance on the left; and the pass puts out about a quarter of a cubic metre a second into a river carrying nine, so four metres from the mouth there is nothing left to lead a fish across. Of the 174 tagged dace that reached the weir, only twenty-three were read on the entrance side.

B is the explanation the passage opens with and then takes apart. It is the natural one, which is why it is here: a dace is small and the fall is 270 millimetres. Kelsingham thinks strength has little to do with it, and the tags put the loss earlier. Of the 174 dace that reached the weir, twenty-three got to the entrance side; of the nine that went in, five came out at the top. The heavy loss happens before the first wall, not on it.

C is plausible away from the text and absent from it. A pass of this kind is not opened and shut by season, and nothing here suggests the dace run is out of step with anything.

D invents a mechanism that fits the picture of dace moving in loose shoals. It reads well and the text never argues it; the shoaling matters here for where the fish travel, not for whether one will go in alone.

questions.prompt: What is implied about the two orifices cut in 2023?

options.text: The force of the February spate is what packed the lower one.
They were cut to take some of the water out of the notches above them.
The one that stayed clear owes that to sitting higher up the pass.
A fish can now get up the whole pass through walls rather than over them.

questions.rationale:
C is right. Two openings of the same size met the same February spate. The lower one filled to the top and is still full; the one three walls further up came through it clear. Position is the only thing the passage separates them by, so position is what the difference has to be put down to.

A reads the same evidence one step short. It blames the force of the spate, which would have shut both openings; the same water went past the upper one and left it clear, so the force of the spate is not what shut the lower.

B gives the orifices a hydraulic job the passage never gives them. It is the sort of reason an engineer might have, and the text offers a different one: a fish can go through a wall instead of over it.

D reads a change at two walls as a change to the whole pass. There are nine cross-walls, and only two of them were cut in 2023, so a fish still has to go over the other seven. One of those two openings has been packed to the top with gravel since February as well, which leaves a fish one wall in nine to go through instead of over.

questions.prompt: What is this text mainly about?

options.text: How many fish an old mill weir still holds back, and what that means for the river above.
An argument that a fish pass should be judged by what comes through it, and a set of counts that supports the case.
What is being done at one weir to get more fish past it, and how little of it has worked.
A pass that one fish gets up easily while two others mostly do not, and the different reason in each case.

questions.rationale:
D is right, and its second half is what the piece is for. Trout go up in thousands, dace and grayling barely at all, and the two failures are not the same failure: the dace are lost outside the pass, on the wrong side of a river, with too little flow out of the entrance to reach them, and the grayling are lost inside it, at drops they cannot leap and in pools with nowhere to rest.

A asks a question the piece never answers. Nothing here counts fish above the weir: the netting that turned up four hundred-odd dace was below it, and the book at the top records what climbed the pass, not what lives upstream. The piece says outright that none of the tagging speaks to the trout, which run in winter. What it establishes is why particular fish fail at particular points, not how much of a river a weir shuts off or what the water above it is missing.

B reads the whole text as a methodological argument about how passes ought to be assessed. It is pitched at the right level of generality, which is why it tempts, and the piece never makes that case: the counts and the tagging are used together to explain a difference, not set against each other as rival tests.

C promotes the last five sentences to the thesis. Two of the nine cross-walls were cut with orifices in 2023, and a second mouth on the right bank is the remedy the argument points to; that is the whole of what the piece says about works, and it comes after the case has been made. The piece is a diagnosis rather than an account of what has been tried, and it delivers no verdict of the kind C attributes to it: one opening packed with gravel and one clear is evidence about position, not a judgement on whether the cutting was worth doing.
